Mincing
MIN-sing
verb
From the Old French mincier, “to cut small,” from a Late Latin minutiare, from minutus, “small”; hence to walk with short, affected, dainty steps — the margin of the KJV reads “tripping nicely.”

Biblical Definition

To mince is to walk with short, affected steps — the studied, dainty gait of a woman on display. The word appears once, in Isaiah’s indictment of the daughters of Zion: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isa 3:16). Every clause is a posture. The neck is stretched out, the eyes deceive as they glance, the steps are cut small and studied, and ankle-chains chime at every pace so that no one may fail to notice her coming. This is not beauty; it is advertisement, and the LORD reads it as haughtiness, the heart’s pride worked out into a walk. The judgment answers the sin exactly. “Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts” (Isa 3:17); and He goes on to strip away the whole inventory — “the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon” (Isa 3:18) — ornament by ornament, for twenty verses. What was flaunted is uncovered; what was displayed is taken away. Against the mincing walk Scripture sets the apostolic order for godly women: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1Ti 2:9). The daughters of Zion made an ornament of themselves; the daughters of the King are adorned with the fear of the LORD, and that beauty judgment cannot strip away.

Webster 1828 Definition

Walking with short, affected, dainty steps; the studied gait of display — the KJV margin, “tripping nicely.”

expand to see more

MINCE, to walk with short steps; to affect a dainty, studied gait.

From the Old French mincier, “to cut small” — the steps are cut short.

The KJV margin at Isa 3:16 reads “tripping nicely.”

The daughters of Zion walked mincing, with stretched necks and tinkling feet.

Isaiah names the gait haughtiness, and the LORD strips away the finery that fed it (Isa 3:18).

Key Scripture

Isa 3:16 — "Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:"

Isa 3:17 — "Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts."

Isa 3:18 — "In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,"

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

Modern Corruption

A live corruption: the mincing walk of Zion is now a whole industry of self-display, and Scripture still names the gait haughtiness.

expand to see more

The corruption is fully alive, and it has been given cameras. Isaiah’s daughters of Zion had stretched necks, wanton eyes, cut and studied steps, and ankle-bells to announce their approach; ours have the same heart and better instruments. The gait is the doctrine: display is not modesty, and the LORD does not read the mincing walk as beauty but as haughtiness — pride worked outward until the body preaches it. And the sin is not in being fair. Isaiah is not against ornament as such; he is against the woman who has made an ornament of herself, and against the men of a city who let her, for the same chapter arraigns Zion’s failed rulers in the very next breath.

The judgment fits the crime with terrible precision. She uncovered herself to be seen, and “the LORD will discover their secret parts”; she flaunted the finery, and the LORD takes away the bravery of the tinkling ornaments, the cauls, the round tires like the moon — twenty verses of inventory, stripped item by item, until the perfume is stench and the girdle a rent. What a woman displays she will lose. Against this Paul sets the order that endures: modest apparel, shamefacedness, sobriety, and good works becoming women professing godliness. Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised — and that adorning no day of visitation can strip away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to walk with short, affected, dainty steps — the gait of display.

expand to see more

Mince — Old French mincier, “to cut small,” from Latin minutus.

The steps are cut short and studied; the KJV margin reads “tripping nicely.”

It denotes an affected, advertising gait, not a natural one.

The daughters of Zion walked mincing, with stretched necks and tinkling feet (Isa 3:16).

The LORD names the walk haughtiness and strips away its ornaments (Isa 3:18).

Usage

"Walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet — the gait was the advertisement."

"The LORD reads the mincing step as haughtiness: pride worked outward till the body preaches it."

"What Zion’s daughters displayed, the day of visitation stripped away, ornament by ornament."
